summary: Defines MIB objects for managing Ethernet-like interfaces. It was a standards-track proposal. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1643.

eli5.summary: A list of gauges for checking Ethernet network cards. It is historic and a newer list replaced it.

subtitle: Standard monitoring objects for Ethernet network interfaces

tldr.problem: Network managers need a standard way to monitor the health and performance of Ethernet interfaces on Internet systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1623 defines a set of managed objects (MIB) that report statistics, errors, collisions and test results for Ethernet-like network interfaces, allowing remote monitoring via SNMP.
tldr.outcome: This became the standard for monitoring Ethernet interfaces, though the specification was later updated and superseded by RFC 1643 with corrections and refinements.

facts.label: Diagnostic tests
facts.value: TDR (cable fault location) and loopback test

today: RFC 1623 is Historic and was superseded by RFC 1643 with corrections and alignment to RFC 1573. It remains the foundational specification for Ethernet interface management via MIB.

sections.title: Introduction to Ethernet-Like MIB
sections.content:
RFC 1623 defines managed objects for monitoring Ethernet-like interfaces in the Internet Management Information Base (MIB). This MIB module lets network managers collect statistics and diagnostic information from Ethernet, StarLAN, and IEEE 802.3 network interface cards using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP).

The document corrects errors from RFC 1398 and aligns the MIB with RFC 1573, which describes how modern interface MIBs should work. The objects are based on the IEEE 802.3 Layer Management specification, which defines how Ethernet devices report their state and performance.
sections.eli5: This is a set of rules for checking on Ethernet network cards. It lets a manager ask "How many packets got through?" and "Did anything go wrong?" using the network.

sections.title: What Networks This Covers
sections.content:
The MIB applies to three types of Ethernet-like interfaces identified by their interface type (ifType) in MIB-II: ethernet-csmacd(6), iso88023-csmacd(7), and starLan(11). All three types are managed identically by this MIB; there are no implementation differences among them.

For each Ethernet-like interface, the MIB objects are indexed by the same index used for that interface in the main Internet-standard MIB (RFC 1213), so a particular Ethernet port can be tracked using a consistent identifier.
sections.eli5: The rules work for three kinds of Ethernet networks. They all use the same ideas, just in different physical wires.

sections.title: Ethernet Statistics
sections.content:
The main statistics group (dot3StatsTable) tracks numerous error and transmission conditions on each interface. This includes alignment errors (frames with incorrect bit length), frame check sequence (FCS) errors (frames with bad checksums), collision-related counts, late collisions (detected 512 bit-times into transmission), excessive collision counts, carrier sense errors, and frames exceeding the maximum size.

The RFC also defines a separate collision statistics group (dot3CollTable) that builds a histogram showing how often frames were transmitted after experiencing exactly 1, 2, 3, or more collisions. This histogram helps diagnose congestion patterns on the network medium.

The MIB also includes the dot3StatsEtherChipSet object, which identifies the MAC (Media Access Control) chip used to implement the interface, allowing managers to correlate statistics with known chip anomalies.
sections.eli5: The tools count how many packets arrived OK, how many had scrambled data, how many had to wait because other packets were being sent, and how confused the hardware got. It's like a car dashboard showing errors and collisions.

sections.title: Testing and Diagnostics
sections.content:
RFC 1623 defines two optional diagnostic tests for Ethernet-like interfaces. The Time-Domain Reflectometry (TDR) test measures the approximate distance to a cable fault by timing the echo of a test pulse; the result is reported in 100-nanosecond units. The loopback test configures the MAC chip to perform an internal self-test of memory, data paths, and logic. The loopback test can only run when the interface is offline.

If a test fails, the RFC defines error identifiers like dot3ErrorInitError (MAC chip could not be initialized for the test) and dot3ErrorLoopbackError (expected data not received during loopback). Many common interface chips do not support one or both tests, so implementation is optional.
sections.eli5: Two special tests help find problems: one bounces a signal down the cable to find breaks, and one tests the card itself when it is unplugged from the network.

sections.title: Relations to Other MIB Standards
sections.content:
RFC 1623 clarifies the relationship between this MIB and RFC 1573 (the Interface MIB Evolution) in several key areas. The MIB does not provide for sublayer support, so there is no layering model; it applies directly to the Ethernet medium. The medium does not support virtual circuits, so that concept does not apply. The ifRcvAddressTable lists all IEEE 802.3 addresses (unicast, multicast, broadcast) that the interface will accept and forward to higher layers.

The specification also explains how the physical address object (ifPhysAddress) should be handled: it contains the IEEE 802.3 address in canonical bit order (with the Group Bit at the low-order position of the first octet). If the address cannot be determined, an octet string of zero length is returned.
sections.eli5: This standard explains how it fits with other rules about network cards. It says: we don't have hidden layers, we don't use virtual circuits, and here's how addresses work.

sections.title: Chipset Identifiers
sections.content:
The document defines a registry of Ethernet MAC chip manufacturer codes for backwards compatibility with pre-RFC 1573 systems. These include identifiers for chips from AMD (7990, 79900, 79C940), Intel (82586, 82596), Seeq (8003), National Semiconductor (8390, Sonic), Fujitsu (86950), and Digital Equipment Corporation (DC21040).

For chipsets not listed in the RFC, the document directs implementors to assign Object Identifiers in other documentation, such as the registration tree delegated to individual enterprises (see RFC 1155). This allows vendors to identify their own proprietary chip implementations without requiring changes to the standard.
sections.eli5: The standard lists codes for different types of Ethernet chips so managers can identify which card is which. If a new chip comes out, vendors can define their own code for it.

fields.name: Alignment Errors
fields.desc: Frames not an integral number of octets and fail FCS.

fields.name: FCS Errors
fields.desc: Frames proper length but fail checksum.

fields.name: Single Collision Frames
fields.desc: Successfully sent after exactly one collision.

fields.name: Multiple Collision Frames
fields.desc: Successfully sent after more than one collision.
